An army captain and Marxist revolutionary who led Burkina Faso from 1983 until he was killed in 1987. He took power in a coup in August 1983, with his friend Blaise Compaoré. In 1984 he renamed the country, then called Upper Volta, Burkina Faso, "land of upright people".

His four years brought fast changes:

  • A vaccination drive that reached millions of children in a few weeks, and campaigns for literacy and public health.
  • Millions of trees planted to hold back the Sahara.
  • Bans on female genital cutting and forced marriage, and women appointed to high office.
  • Lower pay for officials; the government's Mercedes cars were sold and replaced with small Renaults.
  • A call, at the Organisation of African Unity in 1987, for Africa to refuse to pay its foreign debts.

His rule was also harsh: unions and the press were restricted. On 15 October 1987 he was shot dead in a coup that brought Compaoré to power for 27 years. In 2022 a court convicted Compaoré of his murder. Many young Africans see Sankara as a hero, a kind of African Che Guevara.
